cor-closed-convex-halfspaces.title: A Closed Convex Set Is an Intersection of Half-Spaces
cor-closed-convex-halfspaces.title_html: A Closed Convex Set Is an Intersection of Half-Spaces
cor-closed-convex-halfspaces.html: Every non-empty closed convex subset C of V is the intersection of all the closed half-spaces {y:⟨a,y⟩≤c}, with a≠0, that contain C.

cor-duality-certificate.title: Certificates from Weak Duality
cor-duality-certificate.html:
1. If x is feasible for (P), y is feasible for (D), and c⊤x=b⊤y, then x is optimal for (P) and y is optimal for (D).
  2. If (P) is unbounded, then (D) is infeasible. If (D) is unbounded, then (P) is infeasible.

cor-eigenvalue-sums-convex.title: The Top Eigenvalue Sums Are Convex
cor-eigenvalue-sums-convex.title_html: The Top Eigenvalue Sums Are Convex
cor-eigenvalue-sums-convex.html: Let 1≤k≤n. On the real vector space of Hermitian n×n matrices over F, the function sk(A)=λ1(A)+⋯+λk(A) is convex. In particular A↦λ1(A) is convex, and A↦λn(A) is concave.

cor-farkas-inequality.title: Farkas’s Lemma for Inequalities
cor-farkas-inequality.html:
Let M∈Mm×n(R) and d∈Rm. Exactly one of the following has a solution:

  1. Mz≤d with z∈Rn, z≥0;
  2. w≥0, M⊤w≥0 and d⊤w<0, with w∈Rm.

cor-finitely-many-vertices.title: A Polyhedron Has Finitely Many Vertices
cor-finitely-many-vertices.title_html: A Polyhedron Has Finitely Many Vertices
cor-finitely-many-vertices.html: Let P={x∈Rn:Ax≤b} with A∈Mm×n(R). Every vertex of P is the unique solution of AJx=bJ for some set J of n row indices with AJ invertible. In particular P has at most (mn) vertices.

cor-hahn-banach-norm.title: Norm-Preserving Extension
cor-hahn-banach-norm.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional real vector space with a norm ‖⋅‖, let U be a subspace, and let f∈U∗ satisfy |f(u)|≤‖u‖ for every u∈U. Then there is F∈V∗ extending f with |F(v)|≤‖v‖ for every v∈V.

cor-hull-of-compact-is-compact.title: The Hull of a Compact Set Is Compact
cor-hull-of-compact-is-compact.title_html: The Hull of a Compact Set Is Compact
cor-hull-of-compact-is-compact.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional real vector space with a norm, and let K⊆V be compact.

  1. convK is compact.
  2. If K is non-empty, then every linear functional φ on V attains a maximum on convK, and maxx∈convKφ(x)=maxx∈Kφ(x).

cor-linear-max-at-extreme.title: Linear Functions Peak at Extreme Points
cor-linear-max-at-extreme.title_html: Linear Functions Peak at Extreme Points
cor-linear-max-at-extreme.html: Let K⊆V be a non-empty compact convex set and a∈V. Then the maximum of x↦⟨x,a⟩ over K exists and is attained at an extreme point of K. The same holds for the minimum.

cor-lp-optimum-attained.title: Bounded Linear Programs Attain Their Optimum
cor-lp-optimum-attained.title_html: Bounded Linear Programs Attain Their Optimum
cor-lp-optimum-attained.html: If (P) is feasible and its objective is bounded above on the feasible region, that is, c⊤x≤N for some N and every feasible x, then (P) has an optimal solution. The same holds for (D) with “bounded below”.

cor-minkowski-inequality.title: Minkowski’s Inequality
cor-minkowski-inequality.html: Let 1<p<∞. For all x,y∈Rn, ‖x+y‖p≤‖x‖p+‖y‖p. Consequently ‖⋅‖p is a norm on Rn.

cor-norm-as-max.title: A Norm Is a Maximum of Linear Functions
cor-norm-as-max.title_html: A Norm Is a Maximum of Linear Functions
cor-norm-as-max.html: For every norm ‖⋅‖ on Rn and every x∈Rn, ‖x‖=max{⟨x,y⟩:‖y‖∗≤1}, and when x≠0 the maximum is attained at some y with ‖y‖∗=1.

def-affine-hull.title: Affine Combination, Affine Hull
def-affine-hull.html:
Let V be a real vector space.

  1. An affine combination of x1,…,xk∈V, k≥1, is a vector ∑i=1ktixi with real ti satisfying t1+⋯+tk=1. No sign condition is imposed.
  2. An affine subspace of V is a coset p+U of a subspace U (@def-coset). Its dimension is dim⁡U.
  3. The affine hull of S⊆V, written affS, is the set of all affine combinations of points of S.

def-affine-independence.title: Affine Independence
def-affine-independence.html: Let V be a real vector space and let (x0,x1,…,xm) be a list in V, m≥0. The list is affinely independent if, for all real λ0,…,λm, ∑i=0mλixi=0  and  ∑i=0mλi=0⟹λ0=λ1=⋯=λm=0. It is affinely dependent otherwise. A relation ∑iλixi=0 with ∑iλi=0 and the λi not all zero is an affine dependence.

def-basic-feasible-point.title: Active Set, Basic Feasible Point
def-basic-feasible-point.html: Let P={x∈Rn:Ax≤b} and x∈P. The active set of x is I(x)={i:ai⊤x=bi}, the indices of the inequalities that hold with equality at x. The point x is a basic feasible point of the system if among the active rows {ai:i∈I(x)} there are n linearly independent ones.

def-closed-set.title: Closed Set, Open Set
def-closed-set.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional real vector space with a norm, and let K,U⊆V.

  1. K is closed if, whenever (xk) is a sequence of points of K with xk→x for some x∈V, the limit x lies in K.
  2. U is open if, whenever xk→x with x∈U, there is an index N such that xk∈U for every k≥N.

By @cor-convergence-norm-independent (a), both properties are the same for every norm on V. Closedness in (a) is the notion used in @cor-closed-bounded-compact.

def-convex-combination.title: Convex Combination
def-convex-combination.html: Let V be a real vector space and x1,…,xk∈V, with k≥1. A convex combination of x1,…,xk is a vector t1x1+t2x2+⋯+tkxkwith (t1,…,tk)∈Δk, that is, with every ti≥0 and t1+⋯+tk=1.

def-convex-cone.title: Convex Cone
def-convex-cone.html: Let V be a vector space over R. A subset K⊆V is a convex cone if K is non-empty and au+bv∈Kfor all u,v∈K and all real a,b≥0.

def-convex-function.title: Convex Function
def-convex-function.html:
Let C be a non-empty convex subset of a real vector space V, and let f:C→R. Then f is convex if f(tx+(1−t)y) ≤ tf(x)+(1−t)f(y) for all x,y∈C and all real t with 0≤t≤1. It is strictly convex if the inequality is strict whenever x≠y and 0<t<1. It is concave, or strictly concave, if −f is convex, or strictly convex.

The epigraph of f is the subset of the real vector space V×R, with componentwise operations, epif={(x,s)∈V×R:x∈C, s≥f(x)}.

def-convex-hull.title: Convex Hull
def-convex-hull.html: Let S be a subset of a real vector space V. The convex hull of S is the intersection of all convex subsets of V that contain S: convS:=⋂{C⊆V:C is convex and S⊆C}.

def-convex-set.title: Convex Set
def-convex-set.html: Let V be a vector space over R. A subset C⊆V is convex if, for all x,y∈C and every real t with 0≤t≤1, tx+(1−t)y∈C. The set {tx+(1−t)y:0≤t≤1} is the segment joining x and y, written [x,y].

def-density-matrix.title: Density Matrix
def-density-matrix.html: A density matrix of size n is a real symmetric matrix X∈Mn(R) with X⪰0 and trX=1. We write Dn for the set of them.

def-doubly-stochastic.title: Doubly Stochastic Matrix
def-doubly-stochastic.html: A matrix M∈Mn(R) is doubly stochastic if all its entries are non-negative and every row and every column adds up to 1. We write Ωn for the set of doubly stochastic n×n matrices.

def-dual-cone.title: Dual Cone
def-dual-cone.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let S⊆V be any subset. The dual cone of S is S∗={y∈V:⟨x,y⟩≥0 for every x∈S}. We write S∗∗ for (S∗)∗.

def-dual-norm.title: Dual Norm
def-dual-norm.html: Let ‖⋅‖ be a norm on Rn, with closed unit ball B. The dual norm of ‖⋅‖ is the function ‖⋅‖∗:Rn→R given by ‖y‖∗=max{⟨x,y⟩:x∈Rn, ‖x‖≤1}=hB(y).

def-dual-program.title: Dual Program
def-dual-program.html: The dual of the linear program (P) of @def-linear-program is the problem (D)minimize b⊤ysubject toA⊤y≥c,  y≥0, with y∈Rm. The words feasible, infeasible and optimal are used as for (P). (D) is unbounded if it is feasible and b⊤y takes arbitrarily negative values on its feasible region. In this context (P) is called the primal program.

def-extreme-point.title: Extreme Point
def-extreme-point.html: Let C⊆V be a convex set. A point x∈C is an extreme point of C if, whenever x=ty+(1−t)z with y,z∈C and 0<t<1 strictly, then y=z=x. The set of extreme points of C is written extC.

def-face.title: Face
def-face.html: Let C⊆V be convex. A face of C is a convex subset F⊆C such that, whenever ty+(1−t)z∈F with y,z∈C and 0<t<1, both y and z lie in F.

def-finitely-generated-cone.title: Finitely Generated Cone
def-finitely-generated-cone.html: Let a1,…,am be vectors in a real vector space V. The cone generated by them is cone(a1,…,am)={∑i=1mxiai:x1,…,xm≥0}. A cone of this form is finitely generated. For the empty list we set cone()={0}, the value of the empty sum. When V=Rn and A is the matrix with columns a1,…,am, this is {Ax:x∈R≥0m}, and we also write it cone(A).

def-gauge.title: Gauge
def-gauge.html: Let K⊆Rn be convex, with 0 an interior point of K. The gauge (or Minkowski functional) of K is the function pK:Rn→R given by pK(x)=inf{t>0:x∈tK}.

def-interior-point.title: Interior Point, Closure, Boundary Point
def-interior-point.html: Let S⊆V. A point x∈V is an interior point of S if there is a real r>0 such that every y with ‖y−x‖<r lies in S; the set of interior points is written int(S). The closure S― of S is the set of limits of all convergent sequences of points of S. A boundary point of S is a point of S― that is not an interior point of S.

def-linear-program.title: Linear Program
def-linear-program.html: Let A∈Mm×n(R), b∈Rm and c∈Rn. The linear program with these data, in inequality form, is the problem (P)maximize c⊤xsubject toAx≤b,  x≥0. A vector x∈Rn with Ax≤b and x≥0 is a feasible point, and the set of all of them is the feasible region. The program is feasible if it has a feasible point and infeasible otherwise. It is unbounded if it is feasible and c⊤x takes arbitrarily large values on the feasible region. A feasible x⋆ is an optimal solution if c⊤x⋆≥c⊤x for every feasible x, and then c⊤x⋆ is the optimal value.

def-mixed-strategy.title: Mixed Strategy
def-mixed-strategy.html: In the game with payoff matrix A∈Mm×n(R), a mixed strategy for Row is a vector x∈Δm, a mixed strategy for Column is a vector y∈Δn, and the expected payoff is x⊤Ay=∑i=1m∑j=1nxiaijyj.

def-polar-set.title: Polar Set
def-polar-set.html: The polar of a set K⊆Rn is K∘={y∈Rn:⟨x,y⟩≤1 for every x∈K}.

def-polyhedral-cone.title: Polyhedral Cone
def-polyhedral-cone.html: A polyhedral cone in Rn is a set of the form C={x∈Rn:Ax≤0} for some m≥0 and A∈Mm×n(R).

def-polyhedron.title: Polyhedron
def-polyhedron.html: A polyhedron in Rn is a set of the form P={x∈Rn:Ax≤b} for some m≥0, A∈Mm×n(R) and b∈Rm; that is, the intersection of finitely many sets {x:ai⊤x≤bi}. An extreme point of a polyhedron or of a polytope (@def-extreme-point) is called a vertex.

def-polytope.title: Polytope
def-polytope.html: A polytope in Rn is a set of the form conv{v1,…,vk} for finitely many points v1,…,vk∈Rn, k≥0.

def-separation.title: Separation by a Hyperplane
def-separation.html: Let A,B⊆V be non-empty. A non-zero vector a∈V and a number c∈R separate A and B if ⟨a,x⟩≤c≤⟨a,y⟩for all x∈A and all y∈B. They strictly separate A and B if in addition there is a real ε>0 with ⟨a,x⟩≤c−ε and ⟨a,y⟩≥c+ε for all x∈A, y∈B.

def-standard-simplex.title: Standard Simplex
def-standard-simplex.html: For n≥1, the standard simplex in Rn is Δn:={t=(t1,…,tn)∈Rn:ti≥0 for every i,  t1+⋯+tn=1}.

def-sublinear-functional.title: Sublinear Functional
def-sublinear-functional.html: Let V be a real vector space. A function p:V→R is sublinear if, for all x,y∈V and all real t≥0, p(x+y)≤p(x)+p(y)andp(tx)=tp(x).

def-support-function.title: Support Function
def-support-function.html: Let K⊆Rn be non-empty. The support function of K is hK(y)=supx∈K⟨x,y⟩,y∈Rn, with the value +∞ when the numbers ⟨x,y⟩, x∈K, are unbounded above.

def-value-of-game.title: Value and Optimal Strategies
def-value-of-game.html: The number v of @thm-von-neumann-minimax is the value of the game with payoff matrix A, written v(A). A strategy x∈Δm is optimal for Row if it guarantees the value, minyx⊤Ay=v(A), and y∈Δn is optimal for Column if maxxx⊤Ay=v(A).

eq-complementary-slackness.html: b⊤y−c⊤x=y⊤(b−Ax)+x⊤(A⊤y−c).

eq-cone-variational.html: ⟨b−p,z−p⟩≤0for every z∈K.

eq-euclidean-entry-bound.html: |yi| ≤ ‖y‖ ≤ |y1|+⋯+|yn|for y∈Rn and 1≤i≤n.

eq-minimax-saddle.html: x⊤Ay⋆ ≤ v ≤ x⋆⊤Ayfor all x∈Δm, y∈Δn.

eq-strong-duality-certificate.html: A⊤u≥tc,Av≤tb,b⊤u<c⊤v.

eq-strong-duality-system.html: Ax≤b,A⊤y≥c,b⊤y≤c⊤x,x≥0,y≥0.

eq-variational-inequality.html: ⟨x−p,y−p⟩≤0for every y∈C.

exm-caratheodory-reduction.title: Dropping a point in the plane
exm-caratheodory-reduction.title_html: Dropping a point in the plane
exm-caratheodory-reduction.html: In R2 let x0=(0,0), x1=(3,0), x2=(0,3), x3=(2,2), and let x=14(x0+x1+x2+x3)=(54,54). Write x as a convex combination of three of these points by the method of the proof.

exm-caratheodory-sharp.title: The bound is attained
exm-caratheodory-sharp.html: In Rn, let S={0,e1,…,en} and let c=1n+1(0+e1+⋯+en)=1n+11. Show that c∈convS is not a convex combination of any n points of S.

exm-convex-first-examples.title: The first convex sets
exm-convex-first-examples.html:
Check each of the following against @def-convex-set.

  1. The empty set, and a single point {p}.
  2. A subspace U of V, and a coset p+U of it (@def-coset).
  3. A closed half-space {x∈V:φ(x)≤c}, where φ is a non-zero linear functional on V (@def-linear-functional) and c∈R.
  4. A closed ball {x∈V:‖x−p‖≤r} of any norm on V, with center p and radius r≥0.
  5. The set of positive semidefinite matrices (@def-positive-semidefinite) in the real vector space of n×n Hermitian matrices.

exm-cube-cross-polytope.title: The cube and the cross-polytope
exm-cube-cross-polytope.html: For n≥1, describe B∞ and B1 both as polytopes and as polyhedra, and find their vertices from the inequalities by @thm-vertices-basic-feasible.

exm-dual-three-halves-norm.title: A dual norm by hand
exm-dual-three-halves-norm.html: Let y=(3,−4,5)∈R3, and let p=32 and q=3. Compute the dual norm of y with respect to ‖⋅‖3/2, find a vector x with ‖x‖3/2=1 at which it is attained, and compare with the value at the unit vector e3.

exm-extreme-points-not-closed.title: A double cone over a circle
exm-extreme-points-not-closed.title_html: A double cone over a circle
exm-extreme-points-not-closed.html: In R3, let Γ={(1,0,0)+(u,0):u∈R2, ‖u‖=1} be the circle of radius 1 centered at (1,0,0) in the plane x3=0, where (u,0)=(u1,u2,0); it passes through the origin, at u=(−1,0). Let p=(0,0,1), q=(0,0,−1), S=Γ∪{p,q} and K=convS. Show that K is compact and convex, that extK=(Γ∖{0})∪{p,q}, and that this set is not closed.

exm-extreme-points-unit-balls.title: The diamond, the cube and the sphere
exm-extreme-points-unit-balls.title_html: The diamond, the cube and the sphere
exm-extreme-points-unit-balls.html:
In Rn with n≥1, show that:

  1. extB1={±e1,…,±en}, 2n points;
  2. extB∞={s:every si=±1}, the 2n sign vectors;
  3. extB2={x:‖x‖2=1}, the whole unit sphere.

exm-farkas-certificate.title: Deciding a system both ways
exm-farkas-certificate.html: Let A=(120011),b=(32),b′=(−11). Decide, for b and for b′, which alternative of @thm-farkas holds, and exhibit the solution.

exm-first-convex-functions.title: First convex functions
exm-first-convex-functions.html:
Check each against @def-convex-function.

  1. An affine function a(x)=φ(x)+c, with φ a linear functional on V (@def-linear-functional) and c∈R.
  2. A norm ‖⋅‖ on Rn.
  3. f(x)=x2 on R, and more generally q(x)=x⊤Ax on Rn for a symmetric A⪰0.

exm-fourier-motzkin-triangle.title: A triangle, both ways
exm-fourier-motzkin-triangle.html: Let Q=conv{(0,0),(3,0),(0,3),(1,1)}⊆R2. Find a system of inequalities describing Q, and then recover the vertices of Q from it.

exm-game-two-by-three.title: A game with an unused column
exm-game-two-by-three.title_html: A game with an unused column
exm-game-two-by-three.html: Find the value and optimal strategies for the game with payoff matrix A=(3−12−240).

exm-hahn-banach-interval.title: Many extensions
exm-hahn-banach-interval.html: On R2 with ‖⋅‖∞, let U=span((1,1)) and f(s(1,1))=s. Find every F as in @cor-hahn-banach-norm, and compare with the interval produced by the proof of @thm-hahn-banach-finite for v=e1.

exm-helly-four-half-planes.title: Helly’s proof run on four half-planes
exm-helly-four-half-planes.title_html: Helly’s proof run on four half-planes
exm-helly-four-half-planes.html: In R2, let C1={y≥0},C2={x≥0},C3={x+y≤2},C4={x−y≤1}. Find points xi in all the sets except Ci, and follow the proof of @thm-helly to a common point of all four.

exm-hull-membership.title: Deciding membership in a triangle
exm-hull-membership.html: Let p1=(1,0), p2=(3,1), p3=(0,2) in R2. Decide whether x=(54,34) and y=(2,2) lie in conv{p1,p2,p3}.

exm-hull-of-circle.title: Two points suffice for a circle
exm-hull-of-circle.title_html: Two points suffice for a circle
exm-hull-of-circle.html: Let S={x∈R2:‖x‖2=1} be the unit circle. Show that convS is the closed unit disc B2, and that every point of B2 is a convex combination of two points of S.

exm-hyperbola-asymptote.title: A hyperbola and its asymptote
exm-hyperbola-asymptote.html: In R2 with the dot product, let A={x:x1>0, x2>0, x1x2≥1},B={x:x2=0}. Show that A and B are non-empty, disjoint, closed and convex, that the x1-axis is the only hyperplane separating them, and that they are not strictly separated.

exm-image-of-closed-cone-not-closed.title: A closed cone with a non-closed shadow
exm-image-of-closed-cone-not-closed.title_html: A closed cone with a non-closed shadow
exm-image-of-closed-cone-not-closed.html:
In R3, with coordinates (x,y,z), let K={(x,y,z):xs2+2yst+zt2≥0 for all s,t∈R}, the set of triples for which the symmetric matrix (xyyz) is positive semidefinite (@def-positive-semidefinite). Let P=(100010), so that P(x,y,z)=(x,y) is the projection onto the first two coordinates, and write P(K)={Pk:k∈K}. Show that K is a closed convex cone, but that P(K)={(x,y):x>0}∪{(0,0)}, the cone of the earlier warning, which is not closed. Then show that for b=(0,1) neither of the two alternatives holds:

  1. Pk=b for some k∈K;
  2. ⟨Pk,y⟩≥0 for every k∈K, and ⟨b,y⟩<0, for some y∈R2.

exm-lp-workshop.title: The workshop problem, drawn
exm-lp-workshop.html: Find the optimal solution of the workshop problem, and explain why it is optimal.

exm-majorization-set-convex.title: The vectors majorized by a fixed vector
exm-majorization-set-convex.title_html: The vectors majorized by a fixed vector
exm-majorization-set-convex.html: Let 𝛌λ∈Rn. Prove that the set 𝛌{d∈Rn:d≺λ} of vectors majorized by 𝛌λ (@def-majorization) is convex, and deduce that the diagonals of the Hermitian matrices with spectrum 𝛌λ form a convex set.

exm-nearest-point-examples.title: Three projections
exm-nearest-point-examples.html:
Find PC(x) in each case, and check @eq-variational-inequality.

  1. C is the closed unit ball {y:‖y‖≤1} of V, and ‖x‖>1.
  2. C is the box [0,1]3={y∈R3:0≤yi≤1 for each i} with the dot product, and x=(3,−1,2).
  3. C is the half-space {y:⟨a,y⟩≤c}, where a≠0, and ⟨a,x⟩>c.

exm-top-eigenvalue-over-density-matrices.title: The largest eigenvalue as a linear maximum
exm-top-eigenvalue-over-density-matrices.title_html: The largest eigenvalue as a linear maximum
exm-top-eigenvalue-over-density-matrices.html: Let A∈Mn(R) be symmetric. Show that λ1(A)=max{tr(AX):X∈Dn}, and find the maximum for A=(2112).

exm-traffic-lp.title: Capacities on every street
exm-traffic-lp.html: Suppose street 4→1 is open again, but every street can carry at most 35 cars per minute. What is the smallest flow the diagonal street 1→3 can carry, and how would you convince someone that it cannot be smaller?

exm-vertices-quadrilateral.title: The vertices of a quadrilateral
exm-vertices-quadrilateral.html: Find the vertices of P={x∈R2:x1≥0, x2≥0, x1+2x2≤4, 3x1+x2≤6}, and the maximum of φ(x)=x1+x2 over P.

exr-caratheodory-a1.title: A1
exr-caratheodory-a1.html:
1. State @thm-caratheodory.
  2. True or false: every point in the convex hull of ten points of R2 is a convex combination of three of them. Justify your answer.
  3. True or false: the convex hull of a closed subset of R2 is closed. Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: any four points of R3 have a Radon partition. Justify your answer.
  5. Is the list (e1,e2,e3) in R3 affinely independent? Is (e1,e2,e1+e2−e3,e3)?
  6. Which facts from Chapter 15’s list of imported analysis does @cor-hull-of-compact-is-compact use, and where?

exr-caratheodory-b1.title: B1: Shortening a combination
exr-caratheodory-b1.html:
In R2, let x1=(0,0), x2=(4,0), x3=(4,4), x4=(0,4), and x=110x1+210x2+310x3+410x4.

  1. Compute x, and find an affine dependence among x1,…,x4.
  2. Use the method of @thm-caratheodory to write x as a convex combination of three of the points.
  3. Apply the method with the dependence multiplied by −1. Which point is dropped now? Hence x lies in two different triangles with corners among the xi.

exr-caratheodory-b2.title: B2: Radon partitions in the plane
exr-caratheodory-b2.title_html: B2: Radon partitions in the plane
exr-caratheodory-b2.html:
Find a Radon partition, and a point common to the two hulls, for each list of four points in R2. Justify your answer.

  1. (0,0),(4,0),(0,4),(1,1).
  2. (0,0),(3,1),(1,3),(4,4).

exr-caratheodory-b3.title: B3: Linear functionals on a polygon
exr-caratheodory-b3.title_html: B3: Linear functionals on a polygon
exr-caratheodory-b3.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional real vector space with a norm, and x1,…,xm∈V.

  1. Prove that {x1,…,xm} is compact, and deduce that P=conv{x1,…,xm} is compact.
  2. Prove that every linear functional φ on V attains its maximum over P at one of the points xi.
  3. Find the maximum and the minimum of φ(x,y)=2x−y over the triangle conv{(1,0),(3,1),(0,2)} of @exm-hull-membership.

exr-caratheodory-c1.title: C1: Carathéodory in the affine hull
exr-caratheodory-c1.title_html: C1: Carathéodory in the affine hull
exr-caratheodory-c1.html:
Let V be a real vector space, S⊆V non-empty, and suppose affS has dimension d (@def-affine-hull).

  1. Prove that every affinely independent list of points of S has at most d+1 entries.
  2. Hence prove that every point of convS is a convex combination of at most d+1 points of S.
  3. Let S={(t,t,t):0≤t≤1}∪{(2,2,2)}⊆R3. What bound does @thm-caratheodory give, and what bound does (b) give?

exr-caratheodory-c2.title: C2: Helly’s theorem for a sequence of compact sets
exr-caratheodory-c2.title_html: C2: Helly’s theorem for a sequence of compact sets
exr-caratheodory-c2.html:
Let V be a real vector space of dimension n with a norm, and let C1,C2,C3,… be a sequence of compact convex subsets of V such that every n+1 of them have a common point.

  1. Prove that a compact set K is closed.
  2. Prove that for each m≥1 there is a point ym∈C1∩⋯∩Cm.
  3. Prove that ⋂k≥1Ck≠∅.
  4. Explain where the argument fails for the closed half-lines [k,∞) of the remark after @thm-helly.

Hint for (c): all the ym lie in C1.

exr-caratheodory-c3.title: C3: The counts are sharp
exr-caratheodory-c3.html:
Let V be a real vector space of dimension n, and let (x0,…,xn) be affinely independent.

  1. Prove that each point of conv{x0,…,xn} has exactly one expression ∑itixi with t∈Δn+1.
  2. Deduce that 1n+1∑ixi is not a convex combination of any n of the points. (This recovers @exm-caratheodory-sharp.)
  3. Prove that x0,…,xn have no Radon partition, so that n+2 in @thm-radon cannot be lowered.

exr-classical-inequalities-a1.title: A1
exr-classical-inequalities-a1.html:
1. State Young’s inequality, with its hypotheses and its equality case.
  2. Decide whether the following is correct, and justify your answer: the exponent conjugate to p=4 is q=43.
  3. Decide whether the following is correct, and justify your answer: (tr)u=tru for every real t≥0 and all real r,u.
  4. Decide whether the following is correct, and justify your answer: if p,q are conjugate and ⟨x,y⟩=‖x‖p‖y‖q for x,y∈Rn, then one of x,y is a scalar multiple of the other.
  5. Name the convex function to which the proof of @thm-weighted-am-gm applies Jensen’s inequality, and say why the equality case needs it to be strictly convex.

exr-classical-inequalities-b1.title: B1: A dual norm by hand
exr-classical-inequalities-b1.title_html: B1: A dual norm by hand
exr-classical-inequalities-b1.html:
Let y=(1,−6,8)∈R3, and let p=32 and q=3.

  1. Check that p and q are conjugate, and compute ‖y‖3.
  2. Find x∈R3 with ‖x‖3/2=1 and ⟨x,y⟩=‖y‖3.
  3. Hence determine the dual norm of y with respect to ‖⋅‖3/2, and compare it with the value ⟨e3,y⟩ at the unit vector e3.

exr-classical-inequalities-b2.title: B2: Harmonic and arithmetic means
exr-classical-inequalities-b2.html: Let x1,…,xn>0. Prove that n1x1+⋯+1xn ≤ x1+⋯+xnn, with equality if and only if x1=⋯=xn.

exr-classical-inequalities-c1.title: C1: The exponential above its tangent
exr-classical-inequalities-c1.title_html: C1: The exponential above its tangent
exr-classical-inequalities-c1.html:
1. Deduce from @exr-convex-functions-c2 (a) that ey≥1+y for every real y.
  2. Deduce that log⁡x≤x−1 for every real x>0.

exr-classical-inequalities-c2.title: C2: When Hölder is an equality
exr-classical-inequalities-c2.title_html: C2: When Hölder is an equality
exr-classical-inequalities-c2.html:
Let p,q∈(1,∞) be conjugate exponents, and let x,y∈Rn be non-zero.

  1. Prove that ∑i|xiyi|=‖x‖p‖y‖q if and only if |xi|p/‖x‖pp=|yi|q/‖y‖qq for every i.
  2. Deduce that the maximizer in @thm-dual-p-norm is unique: if y≠0, ‖x‖p≤1 and ⟨x,y⟩=‖y‖q, then x is the vector given there.

Hint: in (a), look at where the proof of @thm-holder adds up the inequalities of @lem-young.

exr-cones-and-farkas-a1.title: A1
exr-cones-and-farkas-a1.html:
1. Define a convex cone and the dual cone of a subset S of Rn.
  2. State Farkas’s lemma, and say in one sentence what the vector y in the second alternative certifies.
  3. Determine whether the following is correct, and justify your answer: every convex cone in R2 is closed.
  4. Determine whether the following is correct, and justify your answer: the union of two convex cones in R2 is a convex cone.
  5. In @thm-conic-caratheodory the bound is n generators, while @thm-caratheodory allows n+1 points. Which feature of the proof accounts for the difference?

exr-cones-and-farkas-b1.title: B1: Recognizing cones
exr-cones-and-farkas-b1.html:
Determine which of the following subsets of R2 or R3 are convex cones. Justify your answers.

  1. {x∈R2:x1≥|x2|}.
  2. {x∈R3:x1+x2+x3=0}.
  3. {x∈R2:x1≥1}.
  4. {x∈R2:x2≥x12}.
  5. {x∈R3:x1≥0, x2≥0, x3≤x1+x2}.

exr-cones-and-farkas-b2.title: B2: A certificate either way
exr-cones-and-farkas-b2.html: Let A=(11−1012). For each of b=(0,3) and b=(−1,1), decide which alternative of @thm-farkas holds, and exhibit a solution of that alternative.

exr-cones-and-farkas-b3.title: B3: A dual cone and its dual
exr-cones-and-farkas-b3.title_html: B3: A dual cone and its dual
exr-cones-and-farkas-b3.html:
Let K=cone((1,0),(1,1))⊆R2.

  1. Show that K∗=cone((0,1),(1,−1)).
  2. Compute K∗∗ and check that it equals K, as @thm-dual-cone-of-dual-cone predicts.

exr-cones-and-farkas-c1.title: C1: Gordan’s alternative
exr-cones-and-farkas-c1.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(R).

  1. Prove that exactly one of the following has a solution: Ax=0 with x≥0 and x≠0; or A⊤y>0 with y∈Rm.
  2. Deduce that if the columns of A are (1,0), (0,1) and (−1,−1), then some non-trivial non-negative combination of them is 0, and find one.

Hint for (a): scale x so that its entries sum to 1, and apply @thm-farkas to A with an extra row of ones.

exr-cones-and-farkas-c2.title: C2: The ice-cream cone is its own dual
exr-cones-and-farkas-c2.title_html: C2: The ice-cream cone is its own dual
exr-cones-and-farkas-c2.html:
Let L={(x,t)∈Rn×R:‖x‖2≤t}, with the inner product ⟨(x,t),(y,s)⟩=y⊤x+ts on Rn+1.

  1. Prove that L⊆L∗.
  2. Prove that L∗⊆L.
  3. Deduce that L is closed.

Hint for (b): test (y,s)∈L∗ against the member (−y,‖y‖2) of L.

exr-cones-and-farkas-c3.title: C3: The bidual sees only the closure
exr-cones-and-farkas-c3.title_html: C3: The bidual sees only the closure
exr-cones-and-farkas-c3.html:
Let C={(x,y):x>0}∪{(0,0)}⊆R2, the image cone of @exm-image-of-closed-cone-not-closed.

  1. Prove that C∗={(y1,0):y1≥0}.
  2. Prove that C∗∗={(x,y):x≥0}.
  3. Explain why this does not contradict @thm-dual-cone-of-dual-cone, and show that C∗∗ is the set of all limits of convergent sequences of points of C.

exr-convex-functions-a1.title: A1
exr-convex-functions-a1.html:
1. Define “f is convex on C”, and explain why C is required to be convex.
  2. Decide whether the following is correct, and justify your answer: if f and g are convex on C, then so are f+g and max(f,g).
  3. Decide whether the following is correct, and justify your answer: if f and g are convex on R, then so is their product fg.
  4. Decide whether the following is correct, and justify your answer: a convex function on R is differentiable.
  5. Decide whether the following is correct, and justify your answer: if f:R2→R is convex along every line through the origin, then f is convex.
  6. Name the facts of analysis that the proof of @thm-convex-second-derivative uses.

exr-convex-functions-b1.title: B1: Which are convex?
exr-convex-functions-b1.html:
Determine which of the following functions are convex on the given domain. Justify your answer.

  1. f(x,y)=2x2−2xy+y2 on R2.
  2. f(x,y)=x2+4xy+y2 on R2.
  3. f(x)=max(2x+1, −x, 3) on R.
  4. g(x)=1/x on (0,∞).
  5. g(x)=1/x on {x∈R:x≠0}.

exr-convex-functions-c1.title: C1: Subadditive and homogeneous
exr-convex-functions-c1.html:
Let g:V→R be positively homogeneous: g(tx)=tg(x) for every x∈V and every real t≥0.

  1. Prove that g is convex if and only if g(x+y)≤g(x)+g(y) for all x,y∈V.
  2. Deduce that every norm on Rn is convex, and that @cor-ky-fan-subadditive and @cor-eigenvalue-sums-convex are equivalent statements about sk.

exr-convex-functions-c2.title: C2: Tangent lines
exr-convex-functions-c2.html:
Let I⊆R be an open interval and let g:I→R be differentiable and convex.

  1. Prove that g(y)≥g(x)+g′(x)(y−x) for all x,y∈I.
  2. Deduce that g(y)=maxx∈I(g(x)+g′(x)(y−x)) for every y∈I: a differentiable convex function is the maximum of its tangent lines.

Hint: in (a), apply the definition to the points x and y with weight s on y, and let s→0.

exr-convex-functions-c3.title: C3: Where a convex function is largest
exr-convex-functions-c3.title_html: C3: Where a convex function is largest
exr-convex-functions-c3.html:
1. Let f:Rn→R be convex, and let P be the convex hull conv{x1,…,xm}. Prove that maxx∈Pf(x)=maxif(xi).
  2. Let f(x,y)=x2−xy+y2 and let P be the triangle conv{(2,0),(0,2),(−2,−2)}. Find the maximum and the minimum of f on P, and say where each is attained.

exr-convex-sets-a1.title: A1
exr-convex-sets-a1.html:
1. State @def-convex-set and @def-convex-combination.
  2. True or false: the union of two convex sets is convex. Justify your answer.
  3. True or false: the intersection of two convex sets is convex. Justify your answer.
  4. Explain why the sphere {x∈R3:‖x‖2=1} is not convex, naming the clause that fails.
  5. Describe convS and affS for S={e1,e2}⊆R2.
  6. Give a subset of R that is neither open nor closed, and one that is both.

exr-convex-sets-b1.title: B1: Determine which are convex
exr-convex-sets-b1.html:
Determine which of the following sets are convex. Justify your answer.

  1. {(x,y)∈R2:y≥x2}.
  2. {(x,y)∈R2:xy≥1}.
  3. {A∈M2(R):A⊤=A, detA≥0}.
  4. {x∈R3:x1+2x2−x3=4}.

exr-convex-sets-b2.title: B2: Membership in a hull
exr-convex-sets-b2.html: Let p1=(0,0), p2=(4,1), p3=(1,3) in R2. Decide whether (2,2) and (3,3) lie in conv{p1,p2,p3}. Justify your answer.

exr-convex-sets-c1.title: C1: Midpoint convexity
exr-convex-sets-c1.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional real vector space with a norm, and let C⊆V be midpoint convex: 12(x+y)∈C whenever x,y∈C.

  1. Prove by induction on m that tx+(1−t)y∈C for all x,y∈C and every dyadic t=j/2m with 0≤j≤2m.
  2. Prove that if C is also closed, then C is convex.
  3. Give a midpoint convex subset of R that is not convex, and say which hypothesis of (b) it violates.

Hint for (b): approximate t by ⌊2mt⌋/2m (the floor exists and 2−m→0 by the completeness of R, fact (A1) of Chapter 15’s introduction).

exr-convex-sets-c3.title: C3: Sets that contain lines
exr-convex-sets-c3.html:
Let V be a real vector space and A⊆V a non-empty set containing tx+(1−t)y for all x,y∈A and every real t.

  1. Fix a∈A and put U={x−a:x∈A}. Prove that U is a subspace of V, so that A=a+U is an affine subspace.
  2. Hence prove that a non-empty S⊆V is an affine subspace if and only if S=affS.

Hint for (a): for closure under addition, use a midpoint and then a scaling.

exr-extreme-points-a1.title: A1
exr-extreme-points-a1.html:
1. State the definition of an extreme point of a convex set C⊆V.
  2. True or false: every boundary point of a compact convex set in R2 is an extreme point. Justify your answer.
  3. True or false: there is a non-empty closed convex subset of R2 with no extreme points. Justify your answer.
  4. State @thm-minkowski-extreme, and name the two facts from Chapter 15’s introduction that its proof uses.
  5. True or false: if K=convS with S finite, then every point of S is an extreme point of K. Justify your answer.

exr-extreme-points-b1.title: B1: Finding extreme points
exr-extreme-points-b1.html:
Determine the extreme points of each of the following convex subsets of R2. Justify your answer.

  1. conv{(0,0),(4,0),(0,2),(2,1),(1,1)}.
  2. P={(x,y):x2≤y≤1}.
  3. The strip {(x,y):0≤y≤1}.

Hint: for (b), use @prp-exposed-face (b) with a tangent line.

exr-extreme-points-b2.title: B2: A density matrix split into pure pieces
exr-extreme-points-b2.title_html: B2: A density matrix split into pure pieces
exr-extreme-points-b2.html:
Let X=(1/21/41/41/2),Y=12(1111),Z=(1/2111/2).

  1. For each of the three matrices, decide whether it lies in D2, and if so whether it is an extreme point.
  2. Write X as a convex combination of two extreme points of D2.

exr-extreme-points-b3.title: B3: A doubly stochastic matrix from permutations
exr-extreme-points-b3.title_html: B3: A doubly stochastic matrix from permutations
exr-extreme-points-b3.html:
Let M=16(321132213).

  1. Check that M∈Ω3.
  2. Write M as a convex combination of three permutation matrices. Hence explain why M is not an extreme point of Ω3.

exr-extreme-points-c1.title: C1: Deleting an extreme point
exr-extreme-points-c1.html:
Let C⊆V be convex and x∈C.

  1. Prove that x is an extreme point of C if and only if C∖{x} is convex.
  2. Deduce that x is an extreme point of C if and only if x∉conv(C∖{x}).

exr-extreme-points-c2.title: C2: Every contraction is an average of orthogonal matrices
exr-extreme-points-c2.title_html: C2: Every contraction is an average of orthogonal matrices
exr-extreme-points-c2.html:
Let B={A∈Mn(R):‖A‖2≤1}, the unit ball of the operator 2-norm (@def-operator-norm), so that A∈B exactly when ‖Ax‖≤‖x‖ for every x∈Rn.

  1. Prove that every orthogonal matrix is an extreme point of B.
  2. Prove that every A∈B that is not orthogonal is not an extreme point of B.
  3. Deduce that every A∈B is a convex combination of orthogonal matrices.

Hint for (b): use the singular value decomposition (@thm-svd) and change only the smallest singular value.

exr-extreme-points-c3.title: C3: The corners of the Loewner interval
exr-extreme-points-c3.title_html: C3: The corners of the Loewner interval
exr-extreme-points-c3.html:
Let E={X∈Mn(R):X⊤=X, 0⪯X⪯I}, where X⪯I means I−X⪰0 (@def-loewner-order).

  1. Prove that every symmetric P with P2=P, that is, every orthogonal projection, is an extreme point of E.
  2. Prove that no other point of E is extreme.
  3. Deduce that every X∈E is a convex combination of orthogonal projections, and give such a combination for X=diag(12,14).

Hint for (a): use @lem-psd-form-zero twice, once on kerP and once on imP.

exr-gauges-support-functions-dual-norms-.title: A1
exr-gauges-support-functions-dual-norms-.html:
1. Define the gauge pK, the support function hK and the dual norm ‖⋅‖∗, stating what each needs of the set or norm involved.
  2. Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: the support function of every non-empty bounded subset of R2 is a norm.
  3. What is the dual of ‖⋅‖∞ on Rn? What is the dual of that?
  4. Which result of §03 does the proof of @thm-dual-dual-norm use, and at which point?
  5. Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: K∘∘=K for every non-empty closed convex K⊆Rn.

exr-gauges-support-functions-dual-norms-.title: B1: A weighted norm and its dual
exr-gauges-support-functions-dual-norms-.title_html: B1: A weighted norm and its dual
exr-gauges-support-functions-dual-norms-.html:
On R2 let N(x)=max(|x1|,2|x2|).

  1. Prove that N∗(y)=|y1|+12|y2|.
  2. Verify @thm-dual-dual-norm for N by computing N∗∗ directly.

exr-gauges-support-functions-dual-norms-.title: B2: A hexagonal norm
exr-gauges-support-functions-dual-norms-.html:
Let K={x∈R2:|x1|≤1, |x2|≤1, |x1−x2|≤1}.

  1. Check that K satisfies the hypotheses of @thm-gauge-is-norm (a).
  2. Show that pK(x)=max(|x1|,|x2|,|x1−x2|), and compute pK((2,−1)).
  3. Determine whether pK is induced by an inner product. Justify your answer.

exr-gauges-support-functions-dual-norms-.title: B3: The polar of a triangle
exr-gauges-support-functions-dual-norms-.title_html: B3: The polar of a triangle
exr-gauges-support-functions-dual-norms-.html:
Let K=conv{(−1,−1),(2,−1),(−1,2)}⊆R2.

  1. Compute hK(e1), hK(−e1) and hK((1,1)).
  2. Describe K∘ by three linear inequalities.
  3. Show that (−1,0), (0,−1) and (1,1) lie in K∘, and that (1,0) does not.

exr-gauges-support-functions-dual-norms-.title: C1: The norm from 1 to infinity
exr-gauges-support-functions-dual-norms-.title_html: C1: The norm from 1 to infinity
exr-gauges-support-functions-dual-norms-.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(R), and let ‖A‖1→∞ be the operator norm with ‖⋅‖1 on Rn and ‖⋅‖∞ on Rm.

  1. Using @prp-operator-norm-bilinear (a), prove that ‖A‖1→∞=maxi,j|aij|.
  2. Deduce from @prp-operator-norm-bilinear (b) that the operator norm of A⊤ with ‖⋅‖1 on Rm and ‖⋅‖∞ on Rn is the same number.
  3. Explain why this does not contradict the warning of Chapter 15 §03 that the entrywise maximum is not a matrix norm.

exr-gauges-support-functions-dual-norms-.title: C2: Equivalence constants dualize
exr-gauges-support-functions-dual-norms-.html:
Let N1,N2 be norms on Rn and 0<m≤M constants with mN1(x)≤N2(x)≤MN1(x) for every x.

  1. Prove that 1MN1∗(y)≤N2∗(y)≤1mN1∗(y) for every y.
  2. Apply (a) to ‖x‖2≤‖x‖1≤n‖x‖2 from @prp-p-norm-inequalities, and compare the result with that proposition.

exr-gauges-support-functions-dual-norms-.title: C3: The gauge is the support function of the polar
exr-gauges-support-functions-dual-norms-.title_html: C3: The gauge is the support function of the polar
exr-gauges-support-functions-dual-norms-.html:
Let K⊆Rn be closed and convex, with 0 an interior point.

  1. Prove that pK(x)=hK∘(x) for every x. Hint: for t>0, rewrite “x∈tK” using @thm-bipolar.
  2. Deduce @thm-dual-dual-norm again from (a), @thm-gauge-is-norm (b) and @prp-dual-norm-properties (d).

exr-linear-programming-duality-a1.title: A1
exr-linear-programming-duality-a1.html:
1. Write down the dual of: maximize 2x1+x2 subject to x1+x2≤3, x1−x2≤1, x≥0.
  2. State weak duality and strong duality.
  3. Determine whether the following is correct, and justify your answer: if (P) is infeasible, then (D) is unbounded.
  4. Determine whether the following is correct, and justify your answer: if (P) is feasible and c⊤x≤100 for every feasible x, then (P) has an optimal solution.
  5. At an optimal pair x,y, suppose x2>0. What does complementary slackness say about the second constraint of (D)?

exr-linear-programming-duality-b1.title: B1: Solve and certify
exr-linear-programming-duality-b1.html:
Consider: maximize x1+2x2 subject to x1+x2≤5,−x1+x2≤1,2x1−x2≤4,x≥0.

  1. Sketch the feasible region and guess an optimal solution.
  2. Write down the dual, and use complementary slackness to find a candidate dual solution.
  3. Prove that both candidates are optimal, and state the optimal value.

exr-linear-programming-duality-b2.title: B2: Which case?
exr-linear-programming-duality-b2.html:
For each program, write down its dual, and determine which of the four cases of @thm-strong-duality occurs. Justify your answer, giving the optimal values where they exist.

  1. Maximize x1+x2 subject to x1−x2≤1, x≥0.
  2. Maximize −x1 subject to x1≤2, −x1≤−1, x1≥0.
  3. Maximize x1 subject to x1+x2≤−1, x≥0.

exr-linear-programming-duality-b3.title: B3: A network with one flow
exr-linear-programming-duality-b3.title_html: B3: A network with one flow
exr-linear-programming-duality-b3.html: In the traffic network of this section, close street 4→1 and give every other street a capacity of 30 cars per minute. Show that there is exactly one feasible flow. For its diagonal flow f5=30, give a certificate, in the style of @exm-traffic-lp, that f5≥30 for every feasible flow, and one that f5≤30.

exr-linear-programming-duality-c1.title: C1: The dual of the dual
exr-linear-programming-duality-c1.title_html: C1: The dual of the dual
exr-linear-programming-duality-c1.html:
1. Rewrite (D) as a program in the inequality form of @def-linear-program, with data (−A⊤,−c,−b). Show that the dual of that program, rewritten as a maximization, is (P).
  2. Deduce part (c) of @thm-strong-duality from part (b).

exr-linear-programming-duality-c2.title: C2: Free variables
exr-linear-programming-duality-c2.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(R), b∈Rm, c∈Rn, and consider the program with no sign constraint on x: (Pfree)maximize c⊤x  subject to  Ax≤b.

  1. Prove weak duality between (Pfree) and (Deq): minimize b⊤y subject to A⊤y=c, y≥0.
  2. Writing x=u−v with u,v≥0, show that (Pfree) has the same values as an inequality-form program whose dual is (Deq). Deduce that if both are feasible, both have optimal solutions with equal values.

exr-minimax-a1.title: A1
exr-minimax-a1.html:
1. Define the standard simplex Δn, a mixed strategy, and the value of a matrix game.
  2. State von Neumann’s minimax theorem.
  3. Determine whether the following is correct, and justify your answer: every matrix game has a saddle point in pure strategies.
  4. Explain in two sentences why maxxminyf(x,y)≤minymaxxf(x,y) for every function f for which the extrema exist.
  5. Name the mechanism that produces the equality in @thm-courant-fischer and the one that produces it in @thm-von-neumann-minimax.

exr-minimax-b1.title: B1: A two-by-two game
exr-minimax-b1.html:
Let A=(2−3−11).

  1. Show that the game has no saddle point in pure strategies.
  2. Find the value and optimal strategies for both players, and verify the saddle inequality @eq-minimax-saddle.

exr-minimax-b2.title: B2: A saddle point
exr-minimax-b2.html: Let A=(314201), the second game of this section. Show that x⋆=e1, y⋆=e2 satisfy @eq-minimax-saddle with v=1, and deduce the value of the game.

exr-minimax-b3.title: B3: Many optimal strategies
exr-minimax-b3.html:
Let A=(401−131).

  1. Show that v(A)=1.
  2. Find all optimal strategies for Row.
  3. Show that Column has exactly one optimal strategy.

exr-minimax-c1.title: C1: Symmetric games
exr-minimax-c1.html:
Let A∈Mn(R) be skew-symmetric, A⊤=−A. Such a game is symmetric: the two players have the same options, and swapping their roles swaps the payoff’s sign.

  1. Prove that x⊤Ax=0 for every x∈Rn, and deduce that v(A)=0.
  2. Prove that x is optimal for Row if and only if it is optimal for Column.
  3. In rock–paper–scissors, with the pure strategies in that order and payoff 1 for a win, −1 for a loss and 0 for a tie, A=(0−1110−1−110). Prove that the uniform strategy 131 is the only optimal strategy.

exr-minimax-c2.title: C2: The value depends continuously on the payoffs
exr-minimax-c2.title_html: C2: The value depends continuously on the payoffs
exr-minimax-c2.html:
For A,B∈Mm×n(R), put ε=maxi,j|aij−bij|.

  1. Prove that |v(A)−v(B)|≤ε.
  2. Prove also that if aij≥bij for all i,j, then v(A)≥v(B), and that v(A+cJ)=v(A)+c for every real c.

exr-polytopes-a1.title: A1
exr-polytopes-a1.html:
1. State the definitions of a polytope and of a polyhedron in Rn.
  2. True or false: every polyhedron is a polytope. Justify your answer.
  3. True or false: the intersection of two polytopes in Rn is a polytope. Justify your answer.
  4. State the criterion of @thm-vertices-basic-feasible for a point of {x:Ax≤b} to be a vertex.
  5. True or false: every inequality produced by Fourier–Motzkin elimination (@lem-fourier-motzkin) is needed to describe the projection. Justify your answer.

exr-polytopes-b1.title: B1: Vertices of a pentagon
exr-polytopes-b1.html: Find all vertices of P={x∈R2:x1≥0, x2≥0, x1+x2≤4, x1−x2≤2, −x1+2x2≤5}, and the maximum of 2x1+3x2 over P. Hence write P as a polytope.

exr-polytopes-b2.title: B2: Inequalities for a quadrilateral
exr-polytopes-b2.html:
Use Fourier–Motzkin elimination to find a system of inequalities describing the quadrilateral Q=conv{(0,0),(2,0),(2,1),(0,2)}. Hence find the vertices of Q.

Hint: substitute away t1,t2,t4 and keep s=t3, the weight of (2,1).

exr-polytopes-b3.title: B3: Which of these are vertices?
exr-polytopes-b3.title_html: B3: Which of these are vertices?
exr-polytopes-b3.html:
Let P={x∈R3:x≥0, x1+x2+x3≤3, x1+x2≤2}. Determine which of the following points are vertices of P. Justify your answer.

  1. (0,2,1)
  2. (1,1,1)
  3. (0,0,3)
  4. (3,0,0)
  5. (1,0,0)

exr-polytopes-c1.title: C1: Unbounded polyhedra
exr-polytopes-c1.html:
Let P={x∈Rn:Ax≤b} be a non-empty polyhedron, and let C={(x,t)∈Rn×R:Ax−tb≤0, −t≤0}.

  1. Prove that x∈P if and only if (x,1)∈C.
  2. By @thm-minkowski-weyl (b), C is generated by finitely many vectors (wj,tj), j=1,…,k. Prove that every tj≥0, and that P=conv{wj/tj:tj>0}+{∑tj=0cjwj:cj≥0}, the set of sums of a point of the polytope and a point of the cone. So every non-empty polyhedron is a polytope plus a finitely generated cone.
  3. Check the statement for P={x∈R2:x1≥0, 0≤x2≤1}, with the polytope conv{(0,0),(0,1)} and the cone generated by e1.

exr-polytopes-c2.title: C2: Linear images of polyhedra
exr-polytopes-c2.html:
Let M∈Mp×n(R).

  1. Prove that if P⊆Rn is a polyhedron, then M(P)={Mx:x∈P} is a polyhedron in Rp, and that if P is a polyhedral cone, so is M(P).
  2. Prove that if Q is a polytope, then M(Q) is a polytope, directly from @def-polytope.
  3. Deduce that a linear image of a polyhedral cone is closed. Why does this not contradict the existence of a closed convex cone with a non-closed linear image?

exr-polytopes-c3.title: C3: Vertices in standard form
exr-polytopes-c3.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(R) have columns c1,…,cn, let b∈Rm, and let P={x∈Rn:Ax=b, x≥0}, the feasible region of a linear program in standard form.

  1. Prove that x∈P is a vertex of P if and only if the columns cj with xj>0 are linearly independent.
  2. Deduce that a vertex of P has at most rankA positive entries.
  3. Find the vertices of P={x∈R3:x1+x2+x3=1, x≥0}, the standard triangle.

exr-separation-a1.title: A1
exr-separation-a1.html:
1. State the characterization @eq-variational-inequality of the nearest point, and say what it becomes when C is a subspace.
  2. Which two facts of Chapter 15’s introduction does the existence of PC(x) use, and to which set are they applied?
  3. Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: every non-empty closed subset of R2 has a unique point nearest to 0.
  4. Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: two disjoint non-empty closed convex subsets of R2 can always be strictly separated.

exr-separation-b1.title: B1: Projection onto a half-plane
exr-separation-b1.html: In R2 with the dot product, let C={y:y1+y2≤1} and x=(2,3). Find PC(x) and d(x,C), and verify @eq-variational-inequality.

exr-separation-b2.title: B2: Cutting off a point from a diamond
exr-separation-b2.title_html: B2: Cutting off a point from a diamond
exr-separation-b2.html:
Let C=B1={y∈R2:|y1|+|y2|≤1}, with the dot product, and x=(2,2).

  1. Show that PC(x)=(12,12).
  2. Hence find the strictly separating hyperplane of @thm-separation-point, and check it directly.
  3. Find every supporting hyperplane of C at (12,12).

exr-separation-b3.title: B3: A unique extension
exr-separation-b3.html: On R2 with ‖⋅‖1, let U=span((1,2)) and f(t(1,2))=3t. Show that f satisfies the hypothesis of @cor-hahn-banach-norm, and find every extension F that the corollary allows.

exr-separation-c1.title: C1: The projection does not stretch
exr-separation-c1.title_html: C1: The projection does not stretch
exr-separation-c1.html:
Let C⊆V be non-empty, closed and convex. Prove that ‖PC(x)−PC(y)‖≤‖x−y‖ for all x,y∈V.

Hint: write @eq-variational-inequality once at x, tested with the point PC(y), and once at y, tested with PC(x), and add.

exr-separation-c2.title: C2: Strict separation and distance
exr-separation-c2.html:
Let C1,C2⊆V be non-empty, closed and convex, and put δ=inf{‖y−x‖:x∈C1,y∈C2}.

  1. Prove that if C1 and C2 are strictly separated, then δ>0.
  2. Prove that if δ>0, then C1 and C2 are strictly separated.
  3. Hence deduce, without the computation of @exm-hyperbola-asymptote, that the sets A and B there are not strictly separated.

Hint for (b): replace the difference set D of @thm-separating-hyperplane by its closure.

lem-affine-dependence.title: Affine Dependence by Differences
lem-affine-dependence.html:
Let V be a real vector space and x0,…,xm∈V.

  1. The list (x0,…,xm) is affinely independent if and only if the list (x1−x0,…,xm−x0) is linearly independent.
  2. If dim⁡V=n, every affinely independent list in V has at most n+1 entries. Equivalently, every list of n+2 or more points of V is affinely dependent.

lem-closure-convex.title: Closure and Interior of a Convex Set
lem-closure-convex.title_html: Closure and Interior of a Convex Set
lem-closure-convex.html:
Let C⊆V be convex.

  1. C― is closed and convex.
  2. If z∈int(C), w∈C― and 0<t≤1, then (1−t)w+tz∈int(C).

lem-cone-separation.title: Separating a Point from a Closed Cone
lem-cone-separation.title_html: Separating a Point from a Closed Cone
lem-cone-separation.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional real inner product space, let K⊆V be a closed convex cone, and let b∈V with b∉K. Then there is y∈K∗ with ⟨b,y⟩<0.

lem-convex-contains-combinations.title: Convex Sets Contain Their Convex Combinations
lem-convex-contains-combinations.title_html: Convex Sets Contain Their Convex Combinations
lem-convex-contains-combinations.html: Let C be a convex subset of a real vector space. Then every convex combination of points of C lies in C.

lem-convex-one-variable.title: Increasing Derivative Gives Convexity
lem-convex-one-variable.html: Let I⊆R be an open interval and let g:I→R be differentiable. If g′ is increasing on I, then g is convex; if g′ is strictly increasing, then g is strictly convex. In particular, if g is twice differentiable with g″≥0 on I, then g is convex, and if g″>0 on I, then g is strictly convex.

lem-convex-solid-or-flat.title: A Convex Set Is Solid or Flat
lem-convex-solid-or-flat.title_html: A Convex Set Is Solid or Flat
lem-convex-solid-or-flat.html: Let V≠{0} and let C⊆V be non-empty and convex. Then either C has an interior point, or C lies in an affine hyperplane: there are a≠0 and c∈R with ⟨a,y⟩=c for every y∈C.

lem-exp-log.title: Exponential and Logarithm
lem-exp-log.html:
1. es>0 for every real s, and s↦es is strictly increasing and strictly convex on R.
  2. For every real y>0 there is exactly one real s with es=y; write s=log⁡y.
  3. log:(0,∞)→R is strictly increasing and strictly concave, with log⁡(xy)=log⁡x+log⁡y and log⁡1=0.

lem-extreme-midpoint.title: The Midpoint Test
lem-extreme-midpoint.html: Let C⊆V be convex and x∈C. Then x is an extreme point of C if and only if, whenever x=12(y+z) with y,z∈C, we have y=z.

lem-extreme-points-of-face.title: Extreme Points of a Face
lem-extreme-points-of-face.html: Let C⊆V be convex and F a face of C. Then extF=F∩extC. In particular an extreme point of a face is an extreme point of C.

lem-fourier-motzkin.title: Fourier–Motzkin Elimination
lem-fourier-motzkin.html: Let P={(x,s)∈Rn×R:ai⊤x+cis≤bi for i=1,…,m}. Split the indices by the sign of the coefficient of s: I+={i:ci>0}, I−={i:ci<0}, I0={i:ci=0}. Then π(P) is the set of x∈Rn satisfying ai⊤x≤bifor i∈I0,(ciaj−cjai)⊤x≤cibj−cjbifor i∈I+, j∈I−. In particular π(P) is a polyhedron, and if every bi=0, every right-hand side above is 0.

lem-linear-map-lipschitz.title: Linear Maps Are Lipschitz
lem-linear-map-lipschitz.html: Let V and W be finite-dimensional real vector spaces with norms, and let T:V→W be linear. There is a constant M≥0 such that ‖Tx−Ty‖≤M‖x−y‖for all x,y∈V. In particular xk→x implies Txk→Tx; and every linear functional φ:V→R, with |⋅| as the norm on R, is continuous.

lem-max-min-le-min-max.title: Max–Min Never Exceeds Min–Max
lem-max-min-le-min-max.html: Let X and Y be sets and f:X×Y→R a function for which the extrema below exist. Then maxx∈X miny∈Y f(x,y) ≤ miny∈Y maxx∈X f(x,y).

lem-orthant-image-closed.title: Injective Images of the Orthant Are Closed
lem-orthant-image-closed.title_html: Injective Images of the Orthant Are Closed
lem-orthant-image-closed.html: Let B∈Mn×k(R) have linearly independent columns. Then cone(B)={Bx:x∈R≥0k} is a closed subset of Rn.

lem-psd-form-zero.title: A Zero of the Form Is a Null Vector
lem-psd-form-zero.title_html: A Zero of the Form Is a Null Vector
lem-psd-form-zero.html: Let B∈Mn(R) be symmetric with B⪰0, and let y∈Rn satisfy y⊤By=0. Then By=0.

lem-pure-best-response.title: A Pure Best Response Exists
lem-pure-best-response.html: Let A∈Mm×n(R). For every x∈Δm, miny∈Δnx⊤Ay=min1≤j≤n(A⊤x)j, and the minimum on the left is attained at y=ej for any j attaining the minimum on the right. Likewise, for every y∈Δn, maxx∈Δmx⊤Ay=max1≤i≤m(Ay)i, attained at a vertex ei.

lem-young.title: Young’s Inequality
lem-young.html: Let p,q>1 with 1p+1q=1. Then for all real a,b≥0, ab ≤ app+bqq, with equality if and only if ap=bq.

prp-affine-hull-coset.title: The Affine Hull Is a Coset
prp-affine-hull-coset.title_html: The Affine Hull Is a Coset
prp-affine-hull-coset.html: Let S be a non-empty subset of a real vector space V, let x0∈S, and put U=span{x−x0:x∈S}. Then affS=x0+U, and affS is contained in every affine subspace of V that contains S. In particular U does not depend on the choice of x0∈S.

prp-closed-open-basics.title: Closed and Open Sets: First Facts
prp-closed-open-basics.title_html: Closed and Open Sets: First Facts
prp-closed-open-basics.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional real vector space with a norm.

  1. A subset U⊆V is open if and only if for every x∈U there is a real r>0 with {y∈V:‖y−x‖<r}⊆U.
  2. The intersection of any family of closed sets is closed, and the union of finitely many closed sets is closed.
  3. For a linear functional φ on V and c∈R, the sets {φ≤c}, {φ≥c} and {φ=c} are closed. Every closed ball {x:‖x−p‖≤r} is closed, and every subspace and every coset of a subspace is closed.

prp-convexity-operations.title: Operations Preserving Convexity
prp-convexity-operations.html:
Let V and W be real vector spaces.

  1. The intersection of any family of convex subsets of V is convex.
  2. If T:V→W is linear, C⊆V is convex and D⊆W is convex, then the image T(C) and the preimage T−1(D)={v∈V:Tv∈D} are convex.
  3. If A,B⊆V are convex and c∈R, then A+B, cA and every translate p+A are convex.

prp-dual-cone-basic.title: Basic Properties of the Dual Cone
prp-dual-cone-basic.title_html: Basic Properties of the Dual Cone
prp-dual-cone-basic.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let S,T⊆V.

  1. S∗ is a closed convex cone.
  2. If S⊆T, then T∗⊆S∗.
  3. S⊆S∗∗.
  4. cone(a1,…,am)∗={y:⟨ai,y⟩≥0 for i=1,…,m}. In Rn, with A the matrix of columns ai, this is {y:A⊤y≥0}.

prp-dual-norm-properties.title: Properties of the Dual Norm
prp-dual-norm-properties.html:
Let ‖⋅‖ be a norm on Rn, with closed unit ball B.

  1. ‖⋅‖∗ is a norm on Rn.
  2. |⟨x,y⟩|≤‖x‖‖y‖∗ for all x,y, and ‖y‖∗ is the smallest constant c with |⟨x,y⟩|≤c‖x‖ for every x.
  3. ‖y‖∗ is the operator norm (@def-operator-norm) of the 1×n matrix y⊤, with ‖⋅‖ on Rn and |⋅| on R.
  4. The closed unit ball of ‖⋅‖∗ is the polar B∘.

prp-dual-of-one-two-infinity.title: Duals of the 1-, 2- and Infinity-Norms
prp-dual-of-one-two-infinity.html:
On Rn with the dot product,

  1. the dual of ‖⋅‖1 is ‖⋅‖∞;
  2. the dual of ‖⋅‖∞ is ‖⋅‖1;
  3. the dual of ‖⋅‖2 is ‖⋅‖2.

prp-epigraph-convex.title: Convex Function, Convex Epigraph
prp-epigraph-convex.html: Let C⊆V be non-empty and convex, and let f:C→R. Then f is convex if and only if epif is a convex subset of V×R.

prp-exposed-face.title: Supporting Slices Are Faces
prp-exposed-face.html:
Let C⊆V be convex, let w∈V and α∈R, and suppose ⟨w,x⟩≤α for every x∈C. Then:

  1. F={x∈C:⟨w,x⟩=α} is a face of C;
  2. if F is a single point {c}, then c is an extreme point of C.

prp-extreme-points-of-hull.title: Extreme Points of a Hull Come From the Generators
prp-extreme-points-of-hull.title_html: Extreme Points of a Hull Come From the Generators
prp-extreme-points-of-hull.html: Let S⊆V be any set. Then ext(convS)⊆S.

prp-gauge-properties.title: Properties of the Gauge
prp-gauge-properties.html:
Let K⊆Rn be convex with 0 an interior point, and let x∈Rn.

  1. x∈tK for every t>pK(x).
  2. pK is sublinear (@def-sublinear-functional).
  3. {x:pK(x)<1}⊆K⊆{x:pK(x)≤1}.
  4. If K is closed, then K={x:pK(x)≤1}.

prp-operator-norm-bilinear.title: Operator Norms through Dual Norms
prp-operator-norm-bilinear.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(R), and let ‖⋅‖α, ‖⋅‖β be norms on Rn and Rm, with duals ‖⋅‖α∗ and ‖⋅‖β∗. Then

  1. ‖A‖α→β=max{y⊤Ax:‖x‖α≤1, ‖y‖β∗≤1};
  2. ‖A⊤‖β∗→α∗=‖A‖α→β.

prp-permutation-matrices-extreme.title: Permutation Matrices Are Extreme
prp-permutation-matrices-extreme.html: Every permutation matrix is an extreme point of Ωn.

prp-polyhedron-closed-convex.title: Polyhedra Are Closed and Convex
prp-polyhedron-closed-convex.html: Every polyhedron P={x:Ax≤b} is convex and closed.

prp-sup-of-affine-convex.title: A Supremum of Affine Functions Is Convex
prp-sup-of-affine-convex.title_html: A Supremum of Affine Functions Is Convex
prp-sup-of-affine-convex.html: Let C⊆V be non-empty and convex, and let (ai)i∈I be a non-empty family of affine functions on V. Suppose that for every x∈C the set {ai(x):i∈I} is bounded above, and put g(x)=supi∈Iai(x)(x∈C). Then g:C→R is convex.

prp-support-function-properties.title: Properties of the Support Function
prp-support-function-properties.html:
Let K,L⊆Rn be non-empty and bounded.

  1. hK is sublinear.
  2. If K⊆L, then hK≤hL.
  3. hconvK=hK.

thm-bipolar.title: Bipolar Theorem
thm-bipolar.html: Let K⊆Rn be closed and convex with 0∈K. Then K∘∘=K.

thm-caratheodory.title: Carathéodory’s Theorem
thm-caratheodory.html: Let V be a real vector space with dim⁡V=n, and let S⊆V. Every point of convS is a convex combination of an affinely independent list of points of S. In particular, every point of convS is a convex combination of at most n+1 points of S.

thm-complementary-slackness.title: Complementary Slackness
thm-complementary-slackness.html:
Let x be feasible for (P) and y feasible for (D). Then x and y are both optimal if and only if

  1. for every i, yi>0 implies (Ax)i=bi; and
  2. for every j, xj>0 implies (A⊤y)j=cj.

thm-conic-caratheodory.title: Carathéodory’s Theorem for Cones
thm-conic-caratheodory.html: Let V be a real vector space and let a1,…,am∈V. Every b∈cone(a1,…,am) lies in cone(ai:i∈S) for some set of indices S⊆{1,…,m} such that the list (ai)i∈S is linearly independent. In particular, if dim⁡V=n, then b is a non-negative combination of at most n of the ai.

thm-convex-continuous.title: Convex Functions Are Continuous
thm-convex-continuous.html: Let U⊆Rn be a non-empty open convex set and let f:U→R be convex. Then f is continuous on U. More precisely, for every a∈U there are δ>0 and L≥0 with |f(a+h)−f(a)|≤L‖h‖whenever ‖h‖≤δ.

thm-convex-hull-combinations.title: The Hull Is the Set of Convex Combinations
thm-convex-hull-combinations.title_html: The Hull Is the Set of Convex Combinations
thm-convex-hull-combinations.html: Let S be a subset of a real vector space V. Then convS is the set of all convex combinations of points of S: convS={∑i=1ktixi:k≥1, x1,…,xk∈S, (t1,…,tk)∈Δk}.

thm-convex-second-derivative.title: Convexity from the Hessian
thm-convex-second-derivative.html:
Let U⊆Rn be a non-empty open convex set, and let f:U→R be twice continuously differentiable.

  1. f is convex on U if and only if Hf(a)⪰0 for every a∈U.
  2. If Hf(a)≻0 for every a∈U, then f is strictly convex on U.

thm-dual-cone-of-dual-cone.title: The Bidual of a Closed Cone
thm-dual-cone-of-dual-cone.title_html: The Bidual of a Closed Cone
thm-dual-cone-of-dual-cone.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let K⊆V be a closed convex cone. Then K∗∗=K.

thm-dual-dual-norm.title: The Dual of the Dual Norm
thm-dual-dual-norm.title_html: The Dual of the Dual Norm
thm-dual-dual-norm.html: For every norm ‖⋅‖ on Rn, ‖⋅‖∗∗=‖⋅‖.

thm-dual-p-norm.title: The Dual of the p-Norm
thm-dual-p-norm.html: Let p,q∈(1,∞) be conjugate exponents. On Rn with the standard inner product, the dual norm of ‖⋅‖p is ‖⋅‖q: max{⟨x,y⟩:‖x‖p≤1}=‖y‖q(y∈Rn). For y≠0 the maximum is attained at x with xi=σi|yi|q−1/‖y‖qq−1, where σi=1 if yi≥0 and σi=−1 otherwise.

thm-extreme-density-matrices.title: Extreme Points of the Density Matrices
thm-extreme-density-matrices.title_html: Extreme Points of the Density Matrices
thm-extreme-density-matrices.html: For n≥1, extDn={xx⊤:x∈Rn, ‖x‖=1}, the orthogonal projections of rank one. Every X∈Dn is a convex combination of at most n of them.

thm-farkas.title: Farkas’s Lemma
thm-farkas.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(R) and b∈Rm. Exactly one of the following has a solution:

  1. Ax=b with x∈Rn, x≥0;
  2. A⊤y≥0 and b⊤y<0, with y∈Rm.

thm-finitely-generated-cone-closed.title: Finitely Generated Cones Are Closed
thm-finitely-generated-cone-closed.html: Let a1,…,am∈Rn. Then cone(a1,…,am) is a closed convex cone.

thm-gauge-is-norm.title: Convex Bodies and Norms
thm-gauge-is-norm.html:
1. Let K⊆Rn be closed, bounded, convex and symmetric (−K=K), with 0 an interior point. Then pK is a norm on Rn, and its closed unit ball is K.
  2. Conversely, the closed unit ball B of any norm ‖⋅‖ on Rn is closed, bounded, convex and symmetric, with 0 an interior point, and pB=‖⋅‖.

So the norms on Rn correspond one to one with the sets described in (a).

thm-hahn-banach-finite.title: Hahn–Banach Theorem, Finite-Dimensional
thm-hahn-banach-finite.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional real vector space, let p be a sublinear functional on V, let U be a subspace of V, and let f∈U∗ satisfy f(u)≤p(u) for every u∈U. Then there is F∈V∗ with F(u)=f(u) for every u∈UandF(v)≤p(v) for every v∈V.

thm-helly.title: Helly’s Theorem
thm-helly.html: Let V be a real vector space with dim⁡V=n, and let C1,…,Cm be convex subsets of V, with m≥n+1. If every n+1 of the sets have a point in common, then all m of them have a point in common.

thm-holder.title: Hölder’s Inequality
thm-holder.html: Let p,q∈(1,∞) be conjugate exponents. For all x,y∈Rn, |⟨x,y⟩| ≤ ∑i=1n|xiyi| ≤ ‖x‖p‖y‖q.

thm-jensen.title: Jensen’s Inequality
thm-jensen.html: Let C⊆V be non-empty and convex, and let f:C→R be convex. Let x1,…,xm∈C, and let w1,…,wm≥0 with w1+⋯+wm=1. Then ∑iwixi∈C and f(∑i=1mwixi) ≤ ∑i=1mwif(xi). If f is strictly convex and every wi>0, equality holds only when x1=x2=⋯=xm.

thm-minkowski-extreme.title: Minkowski’s Theorem
thm-minkowski-extreme.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let K⊆V be a compact convex set. Then K=conv(extK). In particular, a non-empty compact convex set has at least one extreme point.

thm-minkowski-weyl.title: Minkowski–Weyl Theorem
thm-minkowski-weyl.html:
1. A subset of Rn is a polytope if and only if it is a bounded polyhedron.
  2. A subset of Rn is a finitely generated cone if and only if it is a polyhedral cone.

thm-nearest-point.title: Nearest Point Theorem
thm-nearest-point.html:
Let C be a non-empty, closed, convex subset of V, and let x∈V.

  1. There is exactly one point p∈C with ‖x−p‖≤‖x−y‖ for every y∈C.

  2. A point p∈C is this nearest point if and only if ⟨x−p,y−p⟩≤0for every y∈C.{#eq-variational-inequality}

thm-radon.title: Radon’s Theorem
thm-radon.html: Let V be a real vector space with dim⁡V=n, and let x1,…,xm∈V with m≥n+2. Then the index set {1,…,m} can be split into two disjoint non-empty sets I and J with conv{xi:i∈I}∩conv{xj:j∈J}≠∅.

thm-separating-hyperplane.title: Separating Hyperplane Theorem
thm-separating-hyperplane.html:
Let C1,C2⊆V be non-empty, disjoint and convex.

  1. If C1 is compact and C2 is closed, then C1 and C2 are strictly separated: there are a≠0 and c with ⟨a,x⟩<c<⟨a,y⟩ for all x∈C1, y∈C2, and indeed with a margin ε>0 as in @def-separation.
  2. In general, C1 and C2 are separated: there are a≠0 and c with ⟨a,x⟩≤c≤⟨a,y⟩ for all x∈C1, y∈C2.

thm-separation-point.title: Separating a Point from a Closed Convex Set
thm-separation-point.title_html: Separating a Point from a Closed Convex Set
thm-separation-point.html: Let C⊆V be non-empty, closed and convex, and let x∉C. Put a=x−PC(x). Then a≠0 and ⟨a,y⟩≤⟨a,x⟩−‖a‖2for every y∈C. In particular a and c=⟨a,x⟩−12‖a‖2 strictly separate C and {x}.

thm-strong-duality.title: Strong Duality for Linear Programs
thm-strong-duality.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(R), b∈Rm and c∈Rn, and let (P) and (D) be as in @def-linear-program and @def-dual-program.

  1. If (P) and (D) are both feasible, then both have optimal solutions, and their optimal values are equal: there are feasible x⋆ and y⋆ with c⊤x⋆=b⊤y⋆.
  2. If (P) is feasible and (D) is infeasible, then (P) is unbounded.
  3. If (D) is feasible and (P) is infeasible, then (D) is unbounded.

thm-support-function-determines.title: The Support Function Determines a Closed Convex Set
thm-support-function-determines.title_html: The Support Function Determines a Closed Convex Set
thm-support-function-determines.html:
Let K,L⊆Rn be non-empty, closed and convex. Then

  1. K={x∈Rn:⟨x,y⟩≤hK(y) for every y∈Rn};
  2. K⊆L if and only if hK(y)≤hL(y) for every y; in particular K=L if and only if hK=hL.

Here hK and hL may take the value +∞, with a≤+∞ for every a.

thm-supporting-hyperplane.title: Supporting Hyperplane Theorem
thm-supporting-hyperplane.html: Let V≠{0}, let C⊆V be convex, and let x0∈V be a point that is not an interior point of C. Then there is a non-zero a∈V with ⟨a,y⟩≤⟨a,x0⟩for every y∈C. If moreover x0∈C, the affine hyperplane {y:⟨a,y⟩=⟨a,x0⟩} passes through x0 and has C in one of its closed half-spaces; it is called a supporting hyperplane of C at x0.

thm-vertices-basic-feasible.title: Vertices Are Basic Feasible Points
thm-vertices-basic-feasible.html: Let P={x∈Rn:Ax≤b} and x∈P. Then x is a vertex of P if and only if x is a basic feasible point.

thm-von-neumann-minimax.title: Von Neumann’s Minimax Theorem
thm-von-neumann-minimax.html: Let A∈Mm×n(R). There are x⋆∈Δm, y⋆∈Δn and v∈R such that x⊤Ay⋆ ≤ v ≤ x⋆⊤Ayfor all x∈Δm, y∈Δn.{#eq-minimax-saddle} Consequently maxx∈Δm miny∈Δn x⊤Ay = v = miny∈Δn maxx∈Δm x⊤Ay, where the outer maximum is attained at x⋆ and the outer minimum at y⋆.

thm-weak-duality.title: Weak Duality
thm-weak-duality.html: If x is feasible for (P) and y is feasible for (D), then c⊤x≤b⊤y.

thm-weighted-am-gm.title: Weighted Arithmetic–Geometric Mean Inequality
thm-weighted-am-gm.html: Let t1,…,tm≥0, and let w1,…,wm>0 with w1+⋯+wm=1. Then t1w1t2w2⋯tmwm ≤ w1t1+w2t2+⋯+wmtm, with equality if and only if t1=t2=⋯=tm.
